title: OpenAI opens the Codex harness to every developer with the Agents API public beta
subtitle: The runtime that powers Codex — session continuity, sandbox, subagents, tool orchestration — is now a single API call, billed through models and container fees rather than a separate agent fee.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: OpenAI launched the Agents API in public beta on September 10, 2026. The API exposes the same harness that runs Codex: long-lived agent sessions, MCP and custom tools, subagent coordination, context compaction across long tasks, and execution inside either an OpenAI-hosted sandbox or a developer-selected compute environment. The beta is open to every API developer, with US data residency and no Zero Data Retention support at launch. Pricing is composed rather than bundled — token usage on the underlying models, tool fees, and hosted-sandbox container fees ranging from three cents for one gigabyte to $1.92 for sixty-four gigabytes per twenty-minute session-container.

The design absorbs into the platform what agent builders have been assembling themselves for two years. Session continuity, tool discovery, parallel tool execution, subagent orchestration, and sandbox integration — the pieces of code every agent framework has had to reinvent — now sit in a managed runtime behind one API. That is a bigger shift than any single model release. It changes what an 'agent framework' has to justify building on top of, and it moves a large fraction of agent code from application-owned to vendor-owned.

The launch also completes a strategy signal OpenAI has been sending since DevDay. The company's September 8 preview of managed agent environments made the direction clear; this week's public beta makes it real. Competitors have parallel plays — Anthropic's managed agents, Google's Agents Development Kit — but OpenAI is now the first to put a production agent runtime in the hands of every paid API developer. Expect the differentiation among agent startups to move fast: harness parity is now table stakes, so the surviving moats will be evaluation, domain data, and the specific tools you can bring.

For learners, the practical takeaway is that the abstraction level of AI development just moved up a step. If you were about to spend two weeks writing session state, tool routing, and sandbox glue, read the API docs first — much of it is now provided. The skills that appreciate in this world are picking the right tools to expose, designing evaluations that catch subagent failures, and knowing when the managed runtime is the right choice versus when you still need to own the loop yourself.
